bib.title: ADAM: A METHOD FOR STOCHASTIC OPTIMIZATION

question: Can a first-order stochastic optimizer using adaptive estimates of gradient first and second moments combine AdaGrad's handling of sparse gradients with RMSProp's handling of non-stationary objectives?
hypothesis: Adam, with bias-corrected moment estimates, converges as fast as or faster than SGD with momentum, AdaGrad, RMSProp, AdaDelta and SFO across convex and non-convex models, and bias correction matters most when beta2 is near 1.
contributions: Adam algorithm (Algorithm 1) with initialization bias correction
O(sqrt(T)) regret bound in the online convex framework
Empirical comparison on logistic regression, MLPs, CNNs and a VAE

method.summary: Adam keeps exponential moving averages of the gradient and squared gradient, bias-corrects both, and updates theta by alpha*m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps). It is compared with SGD-Nesterov, AdaGrad, RMSProp, AdaDelta and SFO on MNIST, IMDB BoW, CIFAR-10 and a VAE, each at its best hyper-parameters from a dense grid.
method.task: stochastic optimization of ML models (logistic regression, MLP, CNN, VAE)

datasets.name: IMDB movie reviews (Maas et al., 2011)
datasets.preprocessing: bag-of-words, first 10,000 most frequent words; 50% dropout noise on BoW features

datasets.name: CIFAR-10
datasets.preprocessing: whitening; dropout on input and fully connected layer

models.name: MLP
models.architecture: two fully connected hidden layers, ReLU

models.name: CNN c64-c64-c128-1000
models.architecture: three alternating stages of 5x5 conv filters and 3x3 max pooling stride 2, then FC layer of 1000 ReLU units

models.name: VAE (Kingma & Welling 2013)
models.architecture: single hidden layer 500 softplus units, 50-dim spherical Gaussian latent

training.objective: MNIST/IMDB: L2-regularized multi-class logistic regression NLL; MLP: cross-entropy with L2 weight decay (deterministic) or dropout; VAE: not stated
training.optimizer: Adam (alpha=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8 defaults); AdaMax alpha=0.002
training.lr: alpha searched over a dense grid per method; VAE log10(alpha) in [-5..-1]
training.epochs: plots: 45 (MNIST LR), 160 (IMDB), 200 (MLP dropout), 45 (CIFAR-10 CNN); VAE 10 and 100
training.weight_decay: L2 weight decay used in MLP and logistic regression; coefficient not stated
training.dropout: 50% on IMDB BoW features; dropout on MLP and CNN (input layer and FC layer for CNN), rate not stated for MLP/CNN

other.init: same parameter initialization used when comparing optimizers
other.hyperparameter_selection: searched over a dense grid, best setting reported (grid values not given)

inference.samples: single run per curve; number of runs/seeds not stated

metrics.name: training cost
metrics.definition: training negative log likelihood / training cost vs iterations over the entire dataset (epochs)

metrics.name: VAE loss
metrics.definition: loss after 10 and 100 epochs vs log10(alpha) for beta1 in {0,0.9}, beta2 in {0.99,0.999,0.9999}, with and without bias correction

baselines: Adam without bias correction (RMSProp with momentum)
eval.protocol: Training-cost curves only; no test accuracy, no multiple seeds or error bars; results reported at best hyper-parameter setting per method.

results.claim: Adam's effective step is bounded (trust region): |delta_t| <= alpha in common cases, a larger bound only for extreme sparsity.
results.quote: The effective magnitude of the steps taken in parameter space at each timestep are approximately bounded by

results.claim: Adam has O(sqrt(T)) regret in the online convex setting, so average regret is O(1/sqrt(T)) and tends to 0.
results.setup: Theorem 4.1/Cor 4.2: alpha_t=alpha/sqrt(t), beta1_t=beta1*lambda^(t-1), bounded gradients and parameter distance, beta1^2/sqrt(beta2)<1; convex only
results.note: Theorem 4.1 (p.5) last term has denominator 2α(1-β1)(1-λ)^2; Theorem 10.5 statement (p.14) matches but the proof's final line (p.15) has 2αβ1(1-λ)^2, an internal inconsistency.

results.claim: Without bias correction, beta2 near 1 gives unstable VAE training, mostly in the first epochs; the best results use small (1-beta2) with bias correction, and Adam is equal or better than RMSProp at every setting.
results.setup: VAE 500 softplus hidden, 50-d latent; beta1 in [0,0.9], beta2 in [0.99,0.999,0.9999], log10(alpha) in [-5..-1]; 10 and 100 epochs
results.quote: Adam performed equal or better than RMSProp, regardless of hyper-parameter setting.

results.claim: SFO is 5-10x slower per iteration than Adam and its memory is linear in the number of minibatches; it failed to converge with dropout.
results.setup: MLP 2x1000 ReLU, MNIST, minibatch 128, deterministic cost with L2 weight decay

results.claim: On MNIST logistic regression Adam converges like SGD-Nesterov, both faster than AdaGrad; on sparse IMDB BoW Adam converges as fast as AdaGrad, both beating SGD-Nesterov by a large margin.
results.setup: batch 128, alpha_t=alpha/sqrt(t); IMDB 10,000-d BoW with 50% dropout
results.quote: Adam converges as fast as Adagrad.

results.claim: On the CIFAR-10 CNN Adam and SGD eventually converge considerably faster than AdaGrad; v_hat vanishes to near zero after a few epochs and is dominated by epsilon, so the first moment matters more.
results.setup: c64-c64-c128-1000 CNN, batch 128, whitened inputs, dropout
results.quote: Adam and SGD eventually converge considerably faster than Adagrad for CNNs

results.claim: AdaMax: replacing the L2 norm by the infinity norm gives u_t = max(beta2*u_{t-1}, |g_t|), needing no bias correction for u, with |delta_t| <= alpha.
results.quote: we don’t need to correct for initialization

limits: Convergence proof covers only convex online learning; the authors state it does not apply to non-convex problems.
Experiments report training cost only, with no test metrics, seeds or variance; best hyper-parameter per method from an unspecified grid.
Dataset sizes, splits, dropout rates, weight decay values, epochs and hardware are not stated.
Authors note the second moment estimate vanishes in CNNs, a poor geometry approximation.
The proof's final line is inconsistent with the theorem statement (see results note).

code.snippet: m_t = beta1*m_{t-1} + (1-beta1)*g_t; v_t = beta2*v_{t-1} + (1-beta2)*g_t^2; m_hat = m_t/(1-beta1^t); v_hat = v_t/(1-beta2^t); theta_t = theta_{t-1} - alpha*m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps)
